newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgaria strikes, Socialists offer vote talks.
newsitem.headline: Bulgaria strikes, Socialists offer vote talks.

text.p: Bulgaria's ruling Socialists, facing mass protests daily and a collapsing economy, appealed on Wednesday for talks with opposition parties to fix a date for early elections.
Interior minister Nikolai Dobrev, struggling to form a new Socialist government, said he would stay in office just three to five months before holding the early vote.

"The chaos and power vacuum may cause a threat to civil peace," he said on state television. "The deadlock is so complicated and the confidence in the government so low that the only alternative is new elections."

The ex-communist Socialists won a four-year term in 1994 but have been caught up in an economic collapse with the lev plummeting, inflation soaring and the government warning of a possible default on a $10 billion foreign debt.
The Socialists have overseen a caretaker government since December when prime minister Zhan Videnov quit after his party suffered a landslide loss in presidential elections.

They have an absolute majority in the 240-seat parliament but the opposition Union of Democratic Forces (UDF) has vowed to try to win over enough Socialist defections to stop Dobrev. The vote must be held in the coming week.
The UDF quickly rebuffed Dobrev's offer for talks to set a vote date -- the third time the ruling Socialists have to shorten the period until an early election.
"There is only one condition under which we will agree to negotiate and that is if Dobrev agrees to give up the mandate (to form a new government)," said UDF deputy Assen Agov.

Pressure on the Socialists has mounted since November when President Petar Stoyanov, a pro-market liberal, won an election landslide. It was seen as a firm repudiation of the Socialists' economic policies.
Students and opposition parties, which have held 24 days of rallies and protests to demand immediate elections, were joined on Wednesday by workers who staged widespread support strikes.
Teachers, transport workers, miners, hospital staff and factory workers around Bulgaria stopped work during the day for an hour or more to back anti-government protests.
Train services in the Black Sea Bourgas region and in the second city of Plovdiv were halted. The highway to the Danube port of Rousse was blocked with blazing tyres.
Many plants stopped work during the day. Opposition party supporters blocked the main Bulgaria-Greece highway and said it would stay shut until elections were called.
Underscoring the depth of the crisis, Stoyanov said during a visit to Brussels that Bulgaria may have to default on debt repayments unless it receives badly needed financial help.
Organisations such as the International Monetary Fund (IMF) have withheld credit to Bulgaria, saying the Socialists failed to embrace reform after their election in December 1994.
The IMF is withholding a $115 million credit, saying that it wants to see action on closing loss-making state companies and privatisation.

Students and the UDF have staged colourful protests since January 6 to pressure the government to quit. Taxis joined in the festivities on Wednesday, with hundreds of Russian-made Lada cabs racing through Sofia hooting horns and waving flags.
Students held a candle-light parade and a spoof Miss Protest and Mr Vagabond contest -- critics have refered to the youthful protesters as "mere vagabonds".
To a rock version of the national anthem, women students paraded in military uniforms or just lingerie under coats and boasted names such as Miss Kalashnikova or Miss Flakjacket.
Aside from student gaiety, the public's mood has been grim. The main branch of the State Savings Bank was swamped with people trying to withdraw money -- losing its value by the hour.

"I am fed up with all this chaos," said Michail Shopov. "I do not care that the dollar is at 1,500 levs now. Last week, when I could buy dollars at 800-900, I decided to wait for some time and I was wrong."
